summary: Added try/catch rollback block in createProject(): wraps fs.mkdirSync() and workspaceOrchestrator.createWorkspace() calls; on any throw, calls this.projectManager.remove(project.Id) then re-throws.

Added path-traversal guard in renameProject() as the very first operation after the existence check (before projectManager.rename()), using path.resolve() + startsWith() against projectsFolder + path.sep.

Ordering insight: the guard must precede projectManager.rename() because that method validates kebab-case format and throws first — placing the guard earlier ensures the security error fires for malicious traversal paths regardless of their format.
Added workspaceOrchestrator to TestFixture interface and makeFixture() return value to support the rollback test.
Added 2 new integration tests: 'createProject rolls back data entry when createWorkspace() fails' and 'renameProject throws with Security check failed for a path-traversal newId'.

comments.note: The path-traversal guard in deleteProject() (line 109) appends a trailing period to its error message ('...projectsFolder "...".') while the new guard in renameProject() does not. Minor inconsistency — neither form is wrong, but aligning punctuation would make the messages uniform.

renameProject() now has a subtle semantic gap: the path-traversal guard fires before projectManager.rename() validates kebab-case. A traversal path like '../../valid-id' would pass the guard and then be rejected by the manager's format check. This is the correct priority (security before business rules), but the JSDoc on the method lists the throws in the wrong order — it should document the security throw first.

WorkspaceOrchestrator.createWorkspace() is not declared as an arrow function / bound method, so the monkey-patching approach used in the rollback test (replacing the method on the instance) works fine here. However, if createWorkspace() were ever made private or sealed, the test approach would break. A test-seam constructor parameter (e.g. accepting an interface) would be more robust long-term.

comments.note: A04 — Insecure Design / Rollback integrity gap. File: src/orchestration/project-orchestrator.ts, lines 85–89 (createProject catch block). The rollback call this.projectManager.remove(project.Id) is invoked without its own error guard. If remove() throws (e.g., due to a concurrent modification or storage I/O failure), the original error is lost, the stack trace is replaced, and the orphaned data entry is silently left behind — exactly the failure mode the rollback is meant to prevent. In this local CLI context the probability is very low (the entry was just created milliseconds earlier), but wrapping the rollback in its own try/catch and re-throwing the original error would make the guarantee unconditional. Recommendation: wrap the rollback: try { this.projectManager.remove(project.Id); } catch { /* suppress: best-effort cleanup */ } throw error;

A01 — Path Traversal guard correctness confirmation. Files: project-orchestrator.ts lines 111–120 (deleteProject) and lines 163–172 (renameProject). Both guards use path.resolve() + startsWith(resolvedProjectsFolder + path.sep). The path.sep suffix correctly prevents the sibling-directory bypass attack (e.g., a projectsFolder of /home/user/projects would not match /home/user/projects-evil/). Guard logic is sound and correctly positioned before any filesystem or data-store mutations.

A03 — Injection non-issue confirmation. All filesystem path arguments (fs.mkdirSync, fs.renameSync, fs.rmSync, generateWorkspaceFile, removeWorkspaceFile) are constructed via path.join from a kebab-case-validated projectId. Node built-in fs APIs do not pass arguments through a shell interpreter. No command injection surface exists in the changed code.
No new third-party dependencies introduced by this WP. A06 (Vulnerable Components) check: not applicable.
